name: Ecuadorian Llapingachos (Cheese-Filled Potato Cakes)
region: Tungurahua and Ecuadorian Andes / Kichwa and mestizo foodways
type: Cheese-Filled Potato Cakes / Side or Light Meal
category: Achiote potato cakes filled with cheese
imageAlt: Ecuadorian llapingachos served with chorizo, beet salad and shredded lettuce
imageCredit: Photo: young shanahan, Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 2.0.
summary: Ecuadorian llapingachos turn achiote-tinted mashed potatoes into tender griddled cakes with molten cheese centers, crisp golden faces and optional peanut sauce, avocado and egg.
lead: The success of llapingachos is decided before they reach the griddle: dry, rested potato dough and a cold sealed cake create the contrast between a browned crust and soft cheese-filled center.
about: Llapingachos are thick Ecuadorian potato cakes seasoned with an onion-and-achiote refrito, filled with mild cheese and browned on a flat griddle. They are closely associated with Tungurahua and the central Andes, especially Ambato, but are eaten throughout Ecuador. A full plate may add salsa de maní, fried egg, avocado, chorizo and beet or tomato-onion salad; the cakes also stand alone as a vegetarian side. Ecuador's official tourism authority describes the name as combining Kichwa llapina, 'to crush,' with Spanish gacha, a soft dough or mash, reflecting both the potato base and the shaping action.
story: Potatoes were cultivated in the Andes long before European contact and remain central to Ecuadorian highland cooking. Ecuador Travel identifies llapingachos as a preparation of pre-Hispanic and Creole origin from potato-growing Tungurahua, while the cheese filling, refrito and varied accompaniments show the dish's living, layered development. Ecuadorian cook Layla Pujol documents papa chola as the favored local potato and emphasizes the rest that lets the mash become workable. Market and household plates legitimately differ: some cooks mix cheese through the potato, others enclose it; some serve the cakes beneath peanut sauce and egg, while others pair them with pork, sausage or salad.
caveat: Papa chola and Ecuadorian quesillo are difficult to source outside Ecuador. Floury russet potatoes and low-moisture mozzarella or Oaxaca cheese make a practical home adaptation, but waxy potatoes or very wet fresh cheese produce a looser cake. Do not add flour unless the drained potatoes are still genuinely too soft after resting; excess flour makes the centers heavy. Salsa de maní contains peanuts and must be omitted or clearly labeled for anyone with a peanut allergy. The optional meat accompaniments are not required to identify the dish.
prepNotes: After draining, return the potatoes to the hot empty pot for 2 minutes over low heat. A visibly dry, floury surface creates dough that can be filled without extra flour.
Let the seasoned mash cool for 1 hour before shaping, then chill the filled cakes for 30 minutes. Warm potato sticks; an unchilled cake tends to split when turned.
Use medium heat and leave each cake untouched until its underside is deeply golden and releases from the pan. An early flip tears the soft potato around the cheese.
ingredients: 3 lb russet potatoes, peeled and cut into 2-inch chunks
1 tbsp kosher salt for the cooking water, plus more to taste
2 tbsp neutral oil or achiote oil
1/2 cup finely chopped white onion
1 1/2 tsp ground achiote, omitted if using achiote oil
1/4 tsp ground cumin, optional
8 oz low-moisture mozzarella, Oaxaca cheese or quesillo, grated
2 to 3 tbsp neutral oil, for the griddle
Salsa de maní, for serving, optional
1 ripe avocado, sliced, for serving
6 fried eggs, for serving, optional
Tomato-and-red-onion curtido or cooked beet salad, for serving, optional
steps: Put the potatoes in a large saucepan, cover with cold water by 1 inch and add 1 tablespoon salt. Bring to a boil, reduce to a steady simmer and cook 18 to 25 minutes, until a piece breaks cleanly when pressed with a fork and no firm core remains.

Drain the potatoes thoroughly, return them to the hot empty pot and set over low heat for 2 minutes, shaking once or twice, until the surfaces look dry and chalky. Mash by hand while hot until smooth; do not use a blender or food processor, which makes the starch gluey.

Heat 2 tablespoons oil in a small skillet over medium. Add the onion and cook 4 to 6 minutes, until soft and translucent but not browned. Stir in the ground achiote and optional cumin for 30 seconds, just until the oil turns orange and smells fragrant.

Fold the warm refrito into the mashed potatoes and season with salt. Spread the mash in a wide bowl, cover loosely and let it rest at room temperature for 1 hour. Checkpoint: the cooled mixture should hold a clean thumbprint without sticking heavily; if it is still steamy or slack, give it another 15 minutes.

Divide the potato mixture into 12 equal portions, about a generous 1/3 cup each. Roll one portion into a ball, press a deep well in the center and pack in about 1 1/2 tablespoons grated cheese. Pinch the potato completely over the filling, then flatten gently into a cake about 3 inches wide and 3/4 inch thick.

Set the shaped cakes on a parchment-lined tray. Smooth any cracks with slightly damp fingers so no cheese is exposed, cover and refrigerate for 30 minutes. A well-chilled cake should lift in one piece without sagging over your fingers.

Heat a cast-iron griddle or wide nonstick skillet over medium for 4 minutes. Film it with 1 tablespoon oil. Add only as many cakes as fit with 1 inch between them and cook undisturbed for 4 to 5 minutes, until the bottoms are evenly deep gold and release when a thin spatula is worked underneath.

Turn each cake once, supporting its top with a second spatula if needed. Cook 4 to 5 minutes more, until the second side is browned and the center is hot enough to soften the cheese. Lower the heat if the crust darkens before the sides feel warm.
Transfer the first batch to a rack set over a sheet pan and keep warm in a 225°F oven while cooking the remainder with the additional oil. Do not stack the cakes, which steams away the crust.
Serve two warm llapingachos per person with avocado and the chosen accompaniments. Spoon optional salsa de maní alongside rather than flooding the cakes so their browned surfaces stay crisp.

Refrigerate cooked leftovers within 2 hours for up to 3 days. Reheat in a lightly oiled covered skillet over medium-low until hot through, then uncover for the final minute to restore the crust; freezing can make the potato texture mealy.
sources: Ecuador Travel - official account of llapingachos in Tungurahua, their potato-growing context and Kichwa-Spanish name
Laylita's Recipes - Ecuadorian cook Layla Pujol's llapingacho proportions, resting method and traditional accompaniments

pronunciationDefinition: Ecuadorian griddled potato cakes, typically seasoned with achiote, filled with cheese and served with savory accompaniments.
seoDescription: Make Ecuadorian llapingachos with dry achiote potato dough, sealed cheese centers and crisp griddled crusts, with shaping and flipping checkpoints.
difficultyReason: Requires controlling potato moisture, enclosing cheese without cracks and turning delicate chilled cakes only after a stable crust forms.

name: East Javanese Rawon (Black Kluwek Beef Soup)
imageAlt: East Javanese rawon with rice, tender beef, short bean sprouts, sambal, tempeh and crackers
imageCredit: Photo: Ardhan Febriansyah, Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.
summary: East Javanese rawon slow-simmers beef in an earthy black broth built from safely processed kluwek, shallots, candlenuts, turmeric, galangal, lemongrass and makrut lime leaves.
lead: Rawon's almost black broth should taste layered rather than harsh: properly processed kluwek supplies earthy depth, while a fully fried spice paste and patient simmer turn tough beef tender.
about: Rawon is an East Javanese beef soup immediately recognized by the dark color and savory, earthy flavor of kluwek, the traditionally processed seed of Pangium edule. Surabaya, Malang and Pasuruan all maintain noted versions. Beef brisket, shank or chuck is simmered until tender while a bumbu of kluwek, shallot, garlic, candlenut, turmeric and spices is fried until aromatic, then joined with lemongrass, galangal and makrut lime leaf. Rice, short mung-bean sprouts, fried shallots, sambal, salted duck egg and crackers are common companions, offered separately so each diner balances the bowl.
story: Indonesia's official tourism portal presents rawon as one of East Java's signature dishes and connects its identity to kluwek and the region's aromatic spice paste. The dish has multiple local expressions rather than one fixed formula: Surabaya bowls, Pasuruan's Rawon Nguling and the chile-forward Rawon Setan are among the named styles. Singapore's National Library documents the much older Southeast Asian knowledge behind kluwek itself: raw seeds contain hydrocyanic acid, while boiling, leaching and long fermentation make the black kernel usable in Indonesian, Malay and Peranakan cooking. This recipe begins only with commercially processed culinary kluwek; it does not attempt that specialist detoxification at home.
caveat: Fresh or incompletely processed kluwek can release cyanide and is unsafe. Buy only fermented, ready-to-cook kluwek or packaged kluwek paste from a reputable Indonesian or Southeast Asian food supplier; never forage the fruit or try to detoxify raw seeds at home. Discard a kernel that is pale, moldy, sharply bitter or rancid rather than tasting more of it. Candlenuts are also cooked ingredients, not raw snacks. If verified processed kluwek is unavailable, choose another recipe—the seed is defining, and black food coloring or soy sauce does not make rawon.
prepNotes: Use a product explicitly sold as fermented or processed for culinary use. The kernel should be uniformly dark brown-black and smell earthy, mushroom-like and faintly fermented, never chemical or rancid.
The wet paste will spit at first. Keep stirring until steam subsides, it darkens and oil appears at its edges; this removes raw shallot and turmeric flavors before the paste enters the broth.
Keep the broth at a lazy simmer
Collagen-rich beef becomes tender between gentle bubbles. A rolling boil clouds the soup and tightens the meat before its connective tissue has time to soften.
ingredients: 2 lb boneless beef chuck, brisket or shank, cut into 1 1/2-inch pieces
9 cups water, plus more as needed
2 tsp kosher salt, divided, plus more to taste
8 Asian shallots or 3 large Western shallots, peeled and chopped
5 garlic cloves, peeled
6 commercially processed culinary kluwek nuts, about 3 oz dark flesh, or 3 oz ready-to-use kluwek paste
4 candlenuts, toasted, or 6 unsalted macadamia nuts
1 1/2-inch piece fresh turmeric, peeled, or 1 tsp ground turmeric
1-inch piece fresh ginger, peeled
2 tsp coriander seeds, toasted
1/2 tsp cumin seeds, toasted
1/2 tsp ground white pepper
1/2 tsp cooked shrimp paste, optional
1 tbsp tamarind pulp mixed with 2 tbsp warm water and strained
4 tbsp neutral oil
2 lemongrass stalks, trimmed, bruised and tied in knots
2-inch piece galangal, sliced and bruised
5 makrut lime leaves, torn
2 Indonesian bay leaves, optional
1 tsp grated palm sugar or dark brown sugar
6 cups hot cooked jasmine rice, for serving
2 cups short mung-bean sprouts, rinsed and well drained
Fried shallots, lime wedges and sambal terasi, for serving
3 salted duck eggs, halved, and shrimp or melinjo crackers, optional
steps: Put the beef, water and 1 teaspoon salt in a heavy 6-quart pot. Bring slowly to a boil over medium-high heat, skim the gray foam, then reduce to a bare simmer. Partially cover and cook for 45 minutes while preparing the bumbu.

Crack only commercially processed whole kluwek. Scoop the flesh into a bowl and inspect each piece; discard any pale, moldy or rancid-smelling kernel. Mash the accepted flesh with 1/2 cup warm broth from the pot until it forms a smooth, ink-dark paste. If using ready-to-use paste, loosen it the same way.

Blend the shallots, garlic, kluwek paste, candlenuts, turmeric, ginger, coriander, cumin, white pepper, optional cooked shrimp paste and strained tamarind with 1/3 cup water. Scrape down the jar as needed until no hard candlenut pieces remain.

Heat the oil in a wide skillet over medium. Add the blended bumbu carefully and cook 10 to 14 minutes, stirring and scraping often as it spits. Checkpoint: it is ready when the paste has darkened, the sharp raw-shallot smell has become nutty and aromatic, and small beads of oil collect around the edge.

Add the lemongrass, galangal, makrut lime leaves and optional Indonesian bay leaves to the skillet. Fry 2 minutes more, pressing the aromatics into the paste until the lime and lemongrass aromas are distinct.

Scrape the fried bumbu and aromatics into the beef pot, then rinse the skillet with 1 cup hot broth and add that too. Stir in the palm sugar and remaining 1 teaspoon salt. Return to a lazy simmer, partially cover and cook 60 minutes.

Check the largest beef piece. Continue simmering 20 to 45 minutes, adding hot water if the meat is no longer submerged, until a fork turns easily and the beef separates along its grain with light pressure. The broth should be very dark brown-black with an amber sheen, not thick like gravy.

Remove the lemongrass, galangal and whole leaves. Let the pot settle for 5 minutes, skim only excessive surface fat and taste a cooled spoonful. Adjust salt first; add no more than a pinch of sugar if the broth is harsh rather than balanced and earthy.

Divide hot rice among six bowls or plates and ladle rawon beside or over it. Add a small handful of crisp short bean sprouts and fried shallots. Serve lime, sambal, salted egg and crackers separately so they do not obscure the first taste of the kluwek broth.

Cool leftovers in shallow containers within 2 hours and refrigerate for up to 4 days. The flavor deepens overnight. Reheat to a full simmer, adding a little water if needed; keep fresh sprouts, eggs and crackers separate until serving.
sources: Wonderful Indonesia - official East Java overview of rawon's kluwek broth, spice base, regional styles and accompaniments

seoTitle: East Javanese Rawon Recipe (Black Kluwek Beef Soup)
seoDescription: Cook East Javanese rawon with safely processed kluwek, tender beef and a fully fried aromatic bumbu, with sourcing and doneness checkpoints.
difficultyReason: Requires verifying a specialist processed ingredient, grinding and fully frying a wet bumbu, and holding beef at a controlled simmer until tender.

name: Palestinian Musakhan (Sumac Chicken on Taboon Bread)
region: Palestine / central and northern Palestinian village foodways
type: Sumac-Onion Chicken on Flatbread / Shared Main
category: Roast chicken with sumac onions and taboon bread
imageAlt: Palestinian musakhan portions with roasted chicken, sumac onions, pine nuts and round flatbreads
imageCredit: Photo: Kokaly, Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 3.0.
summary: Palestinian musakhan layers olive-oil-softened onions bright with sumac over taboon bread, crowns them with roasted chicken and finishes the communal platter with toasted pine nuts.
lead: Musakhan depends on generosity and balance: enough olive oil and onion to season the bread, enough sumac to cut that richness, and a final hot assembly that leaves the chicken browned but the taboon supple.
about: Musakhan is a Palestinian shared dish of roast chicken, abundant onions, tart red sumac and olive oil assembled over taboon bread and scattered with pine nuts or almonds. Travel Palestine describes it as a celebration of freshly pressed olive oil; its name means 'something heated or warmed,' referring to the assembled bread and toppings returning to the oven. The bread is not a disposable plate: it absorbs the onion oil and chicken juices while retaining chewy edges, and diners traditionally tear portions from the platter by hand. This home version uses bone-in chicken pieces for even roasting and large sturdy flatbreads when true taboon is unavailable.
story: Musakhan is closely tied to Palestinian village agriculture—wheat for taboon, onions and sumac, chickens raised at home, and olive oil from the annual harvest. Institute for Palestine Studies research describes rural Palestinian food as seasonal, land-based and organized through household work and mutual aid, with bread carrying both daily and cultural importance. On the plate, those relationships are direct: new oil softens a large quantity of onions, the onions season local bread, and the finished tray is shared. Families vary the chicken's initial cook, spice mix, nut garnish and bread format; rolled musakhan is a later portable form, while the broad taboon-based platter remains the reference for this recipe.
caveat: Taboon bread has a chewy, blistered structure designed to absorb oil and juices. Thick Arabic flatbread or naan is a practical substitute, but thin pocket pita can become brittle and should be warmed only briefly. Good culinary sumac should taste tart and fruity, not salty filler; do not use foraged berries unless identified and processed by an expert. The olive oil quantity is characteristic, yet the bread should be saturated at the center rather than swimming. Pine nuts are optional but must be omitted and disclosed for tree-nut allergy. Cook chicken to at least 165°F at the thickest part without touching bone.
prepNotes: Quarter-inch half-moons soften at the same rate. Cook them gently until silky and collapsed but only lightly golden; deeply browned onions lose the dish's fresh sumac contrast.
Season both chicken and onions, then reserve a final spoonful for assembly. Long cooking dulls sumac's color and bright acidity.
Brush and top each loaf only shortly before the final bake. A long wait under wet onions makes the center pasty and prevents the rim from toasting.
ingredients: 6 bone-in, skin-on chicken thighs and 6 drumsticks, about 4 lb total
2 tsp kosher salt, divided, plus more to taste
1 tsp freshly ground black pepper
5 tbsp ground culinary sumac, divided
1 1/2 tsp ground allspice
1/2 tsp ground cinnamon
1/2 tsp ground cumin
3/4 cup extra-virgin olive oil, divided
5 large yellow or red onions, about 2 1/2 lb, halved and sliced 1/4 inch thick
1/2 cup low-sodium chicken broth or water
6 individual taboon breads or 4 large sturdy Arabic flatbreads
1/3 cup pine nuts or slivered almonds
2 tbsp chopped flat-leaf parsley, optional
Plain yogurt and chopped cucumber-tomato salad, for serving, optional
steps: Heat the oven to 425°F with a rack in the upper third. Pat the chicken very dry. Mix 1 teaspoon salt, black pepper, 2 tablespoons sumac, allspice, cinnamon and cumin, then rub the chicken with the spice mixture and 2 tablespoons olive oil, including beneath loose skin where possible.

Arrange the chicken skin-side up on a rimmed sheet pan with space between pieces. Roast 35 to 50 minutes, turning the pan halfway but not the pieces, until the skin is bronze, juices run clear and the thickest thigh reaches at least 165°F without the thermometer touching bone. Transfer the chicken to a plate and reserve every pan juice.

While the chicken roasts, warm 1/2 cup olive oil in a wide heavy skillet over medium-low. Add the onions and 1 teaspoon salt, cover and cook 10 minutes to release their moisture. Uncover and cook 25 to 35 minutes, stirring often, until completely soft, glossy and only lightly golden.

Stir 2 tablespoons sumac into the onions and cook 2 minutes. Add the broth and 3 tablespoons reserved chicken juices, scraping the skillet until the onions are loose and spoonable rather than dry. Taste a cooled spoonful: it should be tart, savory and rich, with no raw-onion bite.
Reduce the oven to 375°F. Spread the pine nuts on a small pan and toast 4 to 7 minutes, shaking once, until pale gold. Transfer them immediately to a cool plate; their residual heat can burn them.

Lay the breads on one or two large sheet pans, overlapping only slightly. Brush each with a little of the remaining olive oil, then divide the warm onions and their oil evenly over the surfaces, leaving a narrow rim. Spoon on enough reserved chicken juice to moisten the centers without creating puddles.

Set the roasted chicken pieces over the onion-covered breads and sprinkle with the final 1 tablespoon sumac. Bake 8 to 12 minutes, until the bread's exposed edges are crisp, its covered center remains flexible and the chicken is hot through.

If the chicken skin needs more color, broil the assembled pans 1 to 2 minutes from at least 6 inches away, watching continuously so the bread and sumac do not scorch. Checkpoint: the onions should glisten and the bread should bend when lifted rather than crack like a chip.

Slide the breads and chicken onto a large platter, scatter with toasted nuts and optional parsley, and spoon over any remaining onion oil. Serve immediately, inviting diners to tear bread beneath each chicken piece; offer yogurt and salad alongside rather than on top.

Remove leftover chicken and onions from the bread before refrigerating within 2 hours. Store them separately for up to 3 days. Reheat the chicken and onions covered to 165°F, then assemble on fresh or briefly warmed bread; fully soaked leftover bread will not regain its original texture.
